Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Handling Missing Modalities

Not every embodiment provides every modality in the shared vocabulary ℳ\mathcal{M} (Sec. 3.1); for example, single-arm embodiments have no left wrist or left end-effector link. EgoX handles such gaps so that token sequences remain semantically aligned across embodiments. For each embodiment ee, the modality indicator

δme=𝕀⁡[m​ is available for ​e]∈{0,1}\delta^{e}_{m}=\mathbb{I}\left[\,m\text{ is available for }e\,\right]\in\{0,1\} (14)

defines the available observation modalities ℳobse={m∈ℳobs:δme=1}\mathcal{M}^{e}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\{m\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{obs}}:\delta^{e}_{m}=1\}, and ℳacte\mathcal{M}^{e}_{\mathrm{act}} is defined analogously. Unavailable observation modalities are omitted from the token sequence in our implementation (Appendix A.2). Alternatively, missing modalities can be kept in the sequence as zero tokens, so that embodiments share the same token layout. In this case, the trunk’s attention adds δme\delta^{e}_{m} to the logits of keys from modality mm, which down-weights the zero tokens without excluding them. Unavailable action modalities are excluded from the action loss (Sec. 3.4).

A.2 Details on MXT+

Modality tokenizers. Each tokenizer ϕme\phi^{e}_{m} maps modality mm to a fixed number LmL_{m} of dd-dimensional tokens. Observation modalities are defined at an anatomical or functional level, e.g., egocentric images, torso pose, left/right wrist poses, and left/right end-effector link poses, so embodiments with different morphologies expose compatible interfaces whenever they share a modality. The exception is embodiment-specific proprioception (hereafter, proprioception), mainly robot and end-effector joint states, whose dimensionality and meaning differ across embodiments. Image modalities are encoded by a visual backbone fvisf_{\mathrm{vis}} shared across all embodiments, followed by an embodiment-specific cross-attention aggregator gmeg^{e}_{m}, so that ϕme=gme∘fvis\phi^{e}_{m}=g^{e}_{m}\circ f_{\mathrm{vis}}. Pose and proprioception modalities are encoded by lightweight MLPs followed by cross-attention aggregation. Only the available modalities are tokenized (Appendix A.1). Their tokens are concatenated in a fixed modality order, together with the current embodiment tokens 𝒁te,dream{\color[rgb]{0.293,0.2305,0.5508}\bm{Z}^{e,\mathrm{dream}}_{t}} produced by the student embodiment tokenizer ϕdreame{\color[rgb]{0.293,0.2305,0.5508}\phi^{e}_{\mathrm{dream}}} from selected modality features (Sec. 3.3):

𝒁te\displaystyle\bm{Z}^{e}_{t} =[(𝒁te,m)m∈ℳobse,𝒁te,dream]∈ℝLe×d,\displaystyle=\big[\,(\bm{Z}^{e,m}_{t})_{m\in\mathcal{M}^{e}_{\mathrm{obs}}},\,{\color[rgb]{0.293,0.2305,0.5508}\bm{Z}^{e,\mathrm{dream}}_{t}}\,\big]\in\mathbb{R}^{L^{e}\times d}, (15)
Le\displaystyle L^{e} =∑m∈ℳobseLm+Ldream.\displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}^{e}_{\mathrm{obs}}}L_{m}+L_{\mathrm{dream}}.

Here 𝒁te,dream∈ℝLdream×d{\color[rgb]{0.293,0.2305,0.5508}\bm{Z}^{e,\mathrm{dream}}_{t}}\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{\mathrm{dream}}\times d} contains current student tokens; the future EMA targets are defined separately in Eq. (6). Tokenizing per modality preserves each modality’s semantic identity and avoids mixing heterogeneous signals too early. The trunk therefore always consumes the same token interface, while the tokenizers absorb embodiment-specific differences in dimensionality, camera availability, and kinematic parameterization.

Shared Transformer trunk. The trunk GθG_{\theta} is an encoder-decoder Transformer. The encoder applies self-attention over 𝒁te\bm{Z}^{e}_{t}, and the decoder cross-attends from NqN_{q} learnable query tokens 𝑸∈ℝNq×d\bm{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{q}\times d} to the encoder outputs:

𝑼te=Gθ​(𝒁te,𝑸)∈ℝNq×d.\bm{U}^{e}_{t}=G_{\theta}\big(\bm{Z}^{e}_{t};\,\bm{Q}\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{q}\times d}. (16)

Because every embodiment is presented through the same token interface, GθG_{\theta} is trained on all embodiments without requiring their raw observations or actions to share a dimensionality. The trunk is therefore the main conduit for cross-embodiment transfer, while the tokenizers and experts retain the embodiment-specific details needed for execution.

Modular action experts. For each available action modality m∈ℳactem\in\mathcal{M}^{e}_{\mathrm{act}}, the action expert decodes the corresponding action chunk from the trunk output:

𝑨^te,m=ψme​(𝑼te)∈ℝH×dme.\hat{\bm{A}}^{e,m}_{t}=\psi^{e}_{m}\big(\bm{U}^{e}_{t}\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{m}^{e}}. (17)

Action modalities are drawn from the shared vocabulary ℳact\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{act}}, so anatomically or functionally corresponding outputs occupy the same modality across embodiments. For example, the wrist pose of a single-arm robot corresponds to the right wrist pose of a bimanual embodiment. The experts remain embodiment-specific to handle differences in control semantics and in which action dimensions an embodiment provides (Appendix A.3), while the structure shared across embodiments is learned by the trunk.

A.3 Training Algorithm

Algorithm 1 details the full EgoX training procedure, including cross-embodiment pretraining, target fine-tuning, embodiment dreaming, and the EMA target update. The rest of this section describes each step, and Table 1 lists the hyperparameters.

Training samples.

A training sample is a time step tt drawn uniformly from the time steps of the training trajectories. It contains the observations 𝒐te\bm{o}^{e}_{t}, the action chunk of the next H=60H=60 steps, i.e., 2 s at 30 Hz, and the observations of the dreaming modalities ℳdreame\mathcal{M}^{e}_{\mathrm{dream}} at the offsets 𝒦={20,40,60}\mathcal{K}=\{20,40,60\}. Chunk steps and dreaming offsets beyond the end of the trajectory are marked as padding, and action dimensions that an embodiment does not provide are marked by its action mask; both are excluded from the losses. For example, end-effector link targets have five fingertip slots per hand, of which G1-Sim-Dex3 uses three, xArm7-Dex4 four, and the grippers of LocoMan-Dex2 and R1Lite-Gripper two (thumb and index); torso-pose components that an embodiment does not control are masked the same way. Non-image observations, actions, and dreaming sources are standardized per embodiment and per field with the mean and standard deviation of that embodiment’s demonstrations.

Embodiment-balanced batches.

In pretraining, every optimizer step draws a mini-batch of BB samples from each embodiment in ℰpre\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{pre}}, so each embodiment contributes the same number of samples to every optimizer step, regardless of dataset sizes. The mini-batches are processed one embodiment at a time, and their gradients are accumulated before a single optimizer step. Because each ℒe\mathcal{L}^{e} is averaged over its own mini-batch, the update follows the sum in Eq. (12). Fine-tuning and training without pretraining draw mini-batches from the target-task data only.

Losses.

The action loss follows Eq. (10) with λme=1\lambda^{e}_{m}=1 for every modality and is computed on standardized actions. The chunk loss ℓact\ell_{\mathrm{act}} uses elementwise smooth L1 with a threshold of 0.05, which is quadratic for errors below the threshold and linear above it. For each modality, valid chunk-step and action-dimension entries are pooled across the embodiment mini-batch before taking the mean. The dreaming loss follows Eq. (8) with λdreame=0.3\lambda^{e}_{\mathrm{dream}}=0.3 and is averaged over all latent tokens at dreaming offsets that are not padded; β=0.01\beta=0.01 for the Kitchen-Bread and Kitchen-Cleanup experiments and β=0.005\beta=0.005 for the Scoop, Insert, and Sort experiments. For the Kitchen-Bread and Kitchen-Cleanup experiments, ℒe\mathcal{L}^{e} also includes a penalty 10−5​max⁡(0,‖𝒛j‖2−100)210^{-5}\max\big(0,\|{\color[rgb]{0.293,0.2305,0.5508}\bm{z}_{j}}\|_{2}-100\big)^{2} on each latent token 𝒛j{\color[rgb]{0.293,0.2305,0.5508}\bm{z}_{j}} produced by the student embodiment tokenizer ϕdreame{\color[rgb]{0.293,0.2305,0.5508}\phi^{e}_{\mathrm{dream}}}, averaged over valid tokens to discourage large token norms. The teachers are exempt from this penalty.

Optimization.

We use AdamW with weight decay 10−410^{-4} and four parameter groups with separate learning rates: the tokenizers, which include the modality tokenizers, the embodiment tokenizers, and any shared image encoder or tokenizer; the trunk; the action experts; and the dreaming experts. All remaining parameters use the trunk learning rate. The tokenizers, trunk, and action experts share one learning rate, 10−410^{-4} in pretraining and in training without pretraining and 5×10−55\times 10^{-5} in fine-tuning, while the dreaming experts use a much smaller one (Table 1). Training uses bfloat16 mixed precision without gradient clipping. Pretraining and training without pretraining use a cosine schedule without warmup: at step tt of a budget of TT steps, every parameter group with initial learning rate η0\eta_{0} uses

ηt=η0​(r+(1−r)​12​(1+cos⁡(π​t/T))),r=0.05,\eta_{t}=\eta_{0}\Big(r+(1-r)\,\tfrac{1}{2}\big(1+\cos(\pi t/T)\big)\Big),\qquad r=0.05, (18)

so each learning rate, including that of the dreaming experts, decays to 5% of its initial value at the end of training. Fine-tuning uses constant learning rates.

Image tokenizer sharing.

MXT+ shares the image encoder across embodiments, while each embodiment keeps its own adapter, i.e., the cross-attention aggregator gmeg^{e}_{m} with its projection and learnable query tokens (Appendix A.2). Encoders are shared per image modality; for example, one encoder processes the egocentric main-camera images of all embodiments. The shared encoder is trained on the images of every embodiment, which pools visual data that is highly imbalanced across embodiments, with human demonstrations making up 49.4% of all trajectories (Table 6), and lets object features learned from one embodiment’s images, such as those of human demonstrations, be reused by the others. The adapters absorb what differs between embodiments: camera placement, field of view, image resolution, and how each embodiment’s own body appears in the image.

EMA teachers.

For each embodiment, the teacher consists of copies of the modality tokenizers of ℳdreame\mathcal{M}^{e}_{\mathrm{dream}} and of the embodiment tokenizer ϕdreame{\color[rgb]{0.293,0.2305,0.5508}\phi^{e}_{\mathrm{dream}}}. The target computation uses the copied feature-encoding components f¯me\bar{f}^{e}_{m}, followed by ϕ¯dreame{\color[rgb]{0.293,0.2305,0.5508}\bar{\phi}^{e}_{\mathrm{dream}}}, as in Eq. (6). When the image encoder or the image tokenizer is shared across embodiments, its teacher copy is shared as well, while each embodiment keeps a teacher copy of any image module it does not share, such as its own aggregator. Teachers receive no gradients. After every optimizer step, their parameters are updated with Eq. (9) using α=0.999\alpha=0.999, and their batch-normalization statistics are copied from the students.

Pretraining.

Each cross-embodiment pretraining run excludes the target embodiment’s demonstrations of the target task, which are used only for fine-tuning. The pretraining-mixture ablations in Sec. 4 follow the same procedure with fewer embodiments in ℰpre\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{pre}}: human-only pretraining uses only human demonstrations, and human-plus-robot pretraining adds demonstrations of the other robots but no data from the target embodiment.

Fine-tuning.

Fine-tuning loads the weights of a pretraining checkpoint, initializes a new optimizer state, and recomputes the per-field mean and standard deviation used for data normalization from the target-task demonstrations. If the target embodiment is in ℰpre\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{pre}}, its tokenizers, action experts, embodiment tokenizer, dreaming expert, and teachers are restored together with the trunk and any shared image encoder or tokenizer. Otherwise, as in the human-only and human-plus-robot ablations, only the trunk and the shared image encoder or tokenizer, if one is used, are transferred, and the modules of the target embodiment are trained from their initialization. Wrist cameras that are not used during pretraining receive new tokenizers whose backbones are initialized from ImageNet. Embodiment dreaming remains active during fine-tuning with the same λdreame⋆\lambda^{e^{\star}}_{\mathrm{dream}} and β\beta.

Training without pretraining and ablations.

MXT+ without pretraining is trained from scratch on the target-task data with the same objective, including embodiment dreaming, and with a private image tokenizer. The MXT ablation removes the embodiment tokenizer, the dreaming expert, and the teachers in both pretraining and fine-tuning, and is otherwise trained with the same recipe as MXT+.

A.4 Baseline Implementations

ACT is trained from scratch and π0.5\pi_{0.5} is fine-tuned from its pretrained checkpoint, both on demonstrations from the target embodiment and task only. Both are deployed with the execution loop and controllers of Appendix A.7, and Table 2 lists their hyperparameters. MXT+ without pretraining and the MXT ablation are described in Appendix A.3.

ACT.

We use the decoder-only variant of ACT (Zhao et al., 2023) introduced in HumanPlus (Fu et al., 2024), which removes the conditional VAE and the encoder–decoder structure of the original model. A single stack of self-attention blocks processes one state token, the image tokens, and 60 learned action queries, and a linear head maps the outputs at the query positions to a chunk of 60 actions. Image tokens are the ResNet-18 feature maps of each camera view, projected to the model width by a 1×11\times 1 convolution and combined with 2D sinusoidal positional embeddings. The two halves of the side-by-side stereo head-camera image are encoded as two views by a shared backbone; in Kitchen-Bread and Kitchen-Cleanup, the two wrist cameras are added as views with their own backbones. States and actions are standardized with dataset statistics. The training loss is an L1 loss on the action chunk, excluding steps padded past the end of an episode, plus an auxiliary feature-prediction loss: the mean squared error between the outputs at the image-token positions and the projected backbone features of the frame 60 steps ahead. ACT has no embodiment tokenizer, action experts, or dreaming expert, and it is not pretrained on other embodiments.

𝝅0.5\pi_{0.5}.

We use the OpenPI implementation of π0.5\pi_{0.5}, initialized from pi05_base. LoRA adapts the language backbone and action expert; the visual encoder, action projections, and time-conditioning MLPs are also trainable. Visual inputs comprise the left stereo view and, for Kitchen tasks, both wrist views, resized with aspect-ratio-preserving padding to 224×224224\times 224. We follow the three-camera interface of the pretrained π0.5\pi_{0.5} model, assigning the left stereo view to the base-camera slot and the wrist views, when available, to their corresponding wrist-camera slots. States are quantile-normalized and discretized into tokens alongside the task instruction. Actions contain wrist poses with fingertip targets for xArm7-Dex4, finger commands for G1-Dex5, or gripper openings for R1Lite-Gripper and LocoMan-Dex2; Z1-Tool predicts wrist poses only. G1 and LocoMan also predict torso commands, and Kitchen policies include base velocities. Simulated Dex3 hands use one closure fraction per hand. Selected pose targets are encoded relative to the current observation; simulated Kitchen-Cleanup uses SO(3) rotation vectors for relative orientations. Actions are quantile-normalized, and state and action tensors are zero-padded to 32 dimensions. The model predicts 60-action chunks and is trained with a flow-matching velocity MSE loss. Standard fine-tuning follows Table 2, with 500 warmup steps and global batch sizes. At deployment, all π0.5\pi_{0.5} policies use real-time chunking (RTC) (Black et al., 2025c), overlapping prediction of the next action chunk with execution of the current chunk to reduce discontinuities. The inference server uses 10 Euler integration steps per chunk. Outputs are unnormalized and converted to embodiment-specific controller commands, executed at 30 Hz.

A.5 Embodiment and Hardware Details

EgoX is evaluated on five physical robot embodiments spanning substantially different morphologies, mobility configurations, and manipulation interfaces, as shown in Fig. 10. The platforms include a bimanual humanoid with dexterous hands (G1-Dex5), a wheeled bimanual mobile manipulator with parallel-jaw grippers (R1Lite-Gripper), a tabletop manipulator with a dexterous hand (xArm7-Dex4), a fixed-base arm equipped with a non-actuated tool (Z1-Tool), and a quadruped with a two-finger gripper (LocoMan-Dex2).

Across all embodiments, EgoX represents manipulation actions using a shared set of semantically corresponding geometric action modalities. These include wrist pose targets and, when available, task-relevant end-effector link pose targets. For dexterous hands and grippers, these links correspond to fingertips, while embodiments that do not provide such structure can use only the applicable subset of action modalities. The predicted geometric targets are mapped to each embodiment’s native control space through embodiment-specific retargeting and low-level control interfaces.

G1-Dex5.

G1-Dex5 is a Unitree G1 humanoid equipped with two Inspire RH56F1 five-finger dexterous hands. EgoX can predict torso pose, left/right wrist pose targets together with five fingertip targets for each hand and optional velocity commands for the whole robot. These geometric targets are retargeted to the corresponding arm and hand control spaces for execution. For locomotion and whole-body stabilization, we use the low-level whole-body controller from Humanoid Touch Dream (Niu et al., 2026), which is kept fixed throughout our experiments.

R1Lite-Gripper.

R1Lite-Gripper is a Galaxea R1 Lite wheeled bimanual mobile manipulator equipped with parallel-jaw grippers. EgoX predicts left/right wrist pose targets together with two fingertip targets for each gripper and optional velocity commands. These geometric targets are mapped to the native arm and gripper control spaces of the R1 Lite for execution. Mobile-base commands are handled through the embodiment-specific locomotion interface.

xArm7-Dex4.

xArm7-Dex4 consists of an xArm7 tabletop manipulator equipped with a four-finger LEAP Hand (Shaw et al., 2023). EgoX predicts a wrist pose target together with four fingertip targets. These geometric targets are retargeted to the xArm7 arm and LEAP Hand control spaces for execution. Since the platform has a fixed base, it does not use a locomotion action modality.

Z1-Tool.

Z1-Tool is a Unitree Z1 tabletop manipulator equipped with a fixed, non-actuated scoop. For this embodiment, EgoX predicts only the wrist pose target, which is executed by the underlying arm controller. Since the scoop is rigidly attached to the arm and has no actuated joints, this embodiment does not predict a separate end-effector keypoint or actuation modality.

LocoMan-Dex2.

LocoMan-Dex2 is a quadrupedal manipulation platform with two-finger grippers mounted on its front legs (Lin et al., 2024). We evaluate the platform in a unimanual configuration. EgoX predicts a wrist pose target together with two fingertip targets for the active gripper. These geometric targets are mapped to the native control space of the active manipulation limb for execution.

A.6 Unified Egocentric Frame System

All frames in EgoX are right-handed, with the xx-axis pointing forward, the yy-axis to the left, and the zz-axis upward, as in IsaacGym and IsaacLab. Table 4 summarizes the frames of each embodiment. The root frame ℱroot\mathcal{F}_{\text{root}} is the reference for the torso pose and the velocity commands. It is the gravity-aligned projection of a reference body part onto the ground that keeps the part’s heading: the head at the start of the episode for human data, and the feet, trunk, chassis, or arm base for robots. Except for the fixed-base arms, the wrist poses in ℱroot\mathcal{F}_{\text{root}} are also provided as observations. The egocentric frame ℱego\mathcal{F}_{\text{ego}} (Sec. 3.1) is rigidly attached to the body that carries the main camera. Wrist poses and wrist targets are expressed relative to it,

𝑻wristego=(𝑻egoroot)−1​𝑻wristroot,{}^{\text{ego}}\bm{T}_{\text{wrist}}=\big({}^{\text{root}}\bm{T}_{\text{ego}}\big)^{-1}\,{}^{\text{root}}\bm{T}_{\text{wrist}}, (19)

where 𝑻BA∈S​E​(3){}^{A}\bm{T}_{B}\in SE(3) is the pose of frame BB in frame AA, and end-effector-link keypoints are expressed in the local frame of each end effector. Poses are stored as a position and roll, pitch, and yaw angles in ZZ–YY–XX order. A fixed rotation brings each robot’s native wrist frame to the EgoX wrist convention, 𝑹wrist=𝑹native​𝑴⊤\bm{R}_{\text{wrist}}=\bm{R}_{\text{native}}\bm{M}^{\top}, where the rows of 𝑴\bm{M} give the native axes that become the EgoX wrist xx-, yy-, and zz-axes (Table 4). Torso-pose components that an embodiment does not use are masked (Appendix A.3).

Human-Dex5.

The headset reports head and wrist poses in its own gravity-aligned tracking frame, whose yy-axis points up; a fixed rotation maps them to the convention above. When the operator starts an episode (Appendix A.8), this frame is rotated about zz by the operator’s head yaw and shifted to the head position, giving a frame with its origin at the head, its xx-axis along the horizontal heading of the head, and its zz-axis opposite to gravity, all taken at the start of the episode. ℱroot\mathcal{F}_{\text{root}} is a pseudo root frame, the projection of this frame onto the ground (Fig. 4). ℱego\mathcal{F}_{\text{ego}} is the tracked head frame, which carries the headset-mounted stereo camera and follows the full head orientation, including pitch and roll. No head-to-torso offset is applied, so the torso modality of human data is the head pose in ℱroot\mathcal{F}_{\text{root}}, with its height measured from the starting head height. The 25 tracked hand keypoints are expressed in the tracked wrist frame, and the fingertips are taken from them.

G1-Dex5.

The controller computes the robot state from the joint encoders by forward kinematics, assuming that both feet are flat on the ground. ℱroot\mathcal{F}_{\text{root}} is the resulting stance frame, recomputed at every control step: its origin is the midpoint of the two ankle-roll links, its zz-axis is the mean of the two foot zz-axes, and its xx-axis is the mean forward direction of the feet, made orthogonal to zz. ℱego\mathcal{F}_{\text{ego}} is a virtual head frame rigidly attached to the torso link, which carries the head and its camera. It has the orientation of the torso link, and its origin lies at (0.154,0,0.406)(0.154,0,0.406) m in torso-link coordinates, i.e., (0.15,0,0.45)(0.15,0,0.45) m from the pelvis when the waist joints are at zero. The torso observation is the torso-link pose in ℱroot\mathcal{F}_{\text{root}}. The torso target is the operator’s head pose in the human ℱroot\mathcal{F}_{\text{root}}: the whole-body controller tracks its orientation as the torso orientation and its height change Δ​z\Delta z since the reset as a torso height of 0.75​m+Δ​z0.75\,\text{m}+\Delta z. Each wrist frame lies 0.05 m beyond the wrist-yaw joint along the joint’s xx-axis. For arm inverse kinematics, wrist targets in ℱego\mathcal{F}_{\text{ego}} are shifted by the same head offset into the pelvis frame.

G1-Sim-Dex3.

The simulated G1 with three-finger Dex3 hands follows the same conventions as G1-Dex5.

R1Lite-Gripper.

The vendor motion-control stack reports the pose of the floating base, the top torso link that carries the stereo head camera and both arms, in the frame of the wheeled chassis, and the end-effector (wrist) poses relative to the floating base. ℱroot\mathcal{F}_{\text{root}} is therefore the chassis frame, and ℱego\mathcal{F}_{\text{ego}} is the floating-base frame. Only the height and pitch of the torso pose are used; the policy predicts no torso target (Table 3), and the chassis is driven by velocity commands. The wrist frames are the vendor end-effector frames, remapped with the same side-specific rotations as G1-Dex5.

LocoMan-Dex2.

The robot is operated in its single-gripper manipulation mode, in which the onboard state estimator expresses the trunk pose relative to the trunk frame at the moment the mode is entered; ℱroot\mathcal{F}_{\text{root}} is the projection of that frame onto the ground. Afterwards, the trunk pose is the rigid transform that aligns the current stance-foot positions, obtained from leg kinematics, with their positions at that moment, so ℱroot\mathcal{F}_{\text{root}} stays fixed to the stance feet. The gripper pose follows from the trunk pose and the forward kinematics of the manipulating leg and its gripper. ℱego\mathcal{F}_{\text{ego}} is the trunk frame, which needs no rotation remap in the unimanual configuration. The height and orientation of the torso pose are used, both measured relative to the trunk frame at mode entry.

xArm7-Dex4.

The arm has a fixed base and a static main camera, so ℱroot\mathcal{F}_{\text{root}} and ℱego\mathcal{F}_{\text{ego}} coincide with the xArm7 base frame, whose xx-axis points forward from the base and whose zz-axis points up. The torso pose is identically zero and is not used. The wrist frame is the joint-7 frame without offset, remapped as in Table 4 for the default reset configuration.

Z1-Tool.

The Z1 also has a fixed base and a static main camera, so ℱroot\mathcal{F}_{\text{root}} and ℱego\mathcal{F}_{\text{ego}} coincide. Both are the Z1 base frame rotated by −90∘-90^{\circ} about zz: the unified xx-axis is the native −y-y-axis, the unified yy-axis is the native xx-axis, and the zz-axis is unchanged. Poses reported by the arm are rotated into this frame, and targets are rotated back before inverse kinematics. The wrist frame is the joint-6 frame without offset or remap. The scoop keypoint lies 0.2 m beyond the joint-6 frame along its xx-axis.

From operator motion to robot targets.

During teleoperation, the operator’s head and wrist poses are first expressed in the human frames above. For G1-Dex5, the wrist poses relative to the head are sent as wrist targets in the robot’s ℱego\mathcal{F}_{\text{ego}}. For the other physical robots, the operator’s head and wrist displacements and rotations since the reset are applied to the robot’s torso and wrist poses at the reset, expressed in the robot’s ℱroot\mathcal{F}_{\text{root}}. For Z1-Tool, these displacements and rotations are scaled by 0.7 and 0.5, respectively.

A.7 Robot Control and Deployment

Shared control stack.

On the physical robots, teleoperation and policy deployment share the same control stack (Fig. 11). A high-level process, either the teleoperation interface or the policy, produces geometric targets in the unified egocentric frame system: wrist pose targets in ℱego\mathcal{F}_{\text{ego}}, end-effector link pose targets in the wrist frames, and, when applicable, torso pose targets in ℱroot\mathcal{F}_{\text{root}} and velocity commands. Fixed, embodiment-specific transforms map these targets to the robot’s base frame and end-effector convention, and the targets are sent over CycloneDDS to an embodiment-specific controller that converts them into joint commands. The controller publishes the robot state back, which is recorded during teleoperation and used as policy input during deployment. Because demonstrations are collected through the same controllers that later execute the policy, recorded actions and policy outputs are interpreted in the same way. Table 5 summarizes the controller of each embodiment.

Policy execution.

At deployment, all methods send actions at 30 Hz, matching the recording rate, and use the same embodiment-specific controllers. MXT+ and ACT predict chunks of 60 actions and execute them open loop without temporal ensembling. By default, these policies execute 60 actions (2 s) before the next query; they execute 45 actions per query in simulation (Appendix A.11), as does pretrained MXT+ on R1Lite-Gripper Kitchen-Bread. The π0.5\pi_{0.5} policies instead use RTC, overlapping prediction of the next chunk with execution of the current chunk (Appendix A.4). An operator can pause the policy or reset the robot from a keyboard at any time.

Arm control.

For G1-Dex5, xArm7-Dex4, and Z1-Tool, wrist pose targets are converted into arm joint targets by inverse kinematics (IK), solved at every control step with Pinocchio (Carpentier et al., 2019) and CasADi (Andersson et al., 2019) using IPOPT (Wächter & Biegler, 2006) with at most 50 iterations. The objective is a weighted sum of the translation error, the rotation error, a joint regularizer, and a smoothness term toward the previous solution, with weights (50,1,0.02,0.1)(50,1,0.02,0.1) for G1-Dex5 and (30,1,0.02,0.2)(30,1,0.02,0.2) for xArm7-Dex4 and Z1-Tool. For G1-Dex5, only the 14 arm joints are optimized and all other joints are locked. Each solution is then smoothed by a weighted moving average over the four most recent solutions, with weights (0.4,0.3,0.2,0.1)(0.4,0.3,0.2,0.1) from newest to oldest. R1Lite-Gripper uses RelaxedIK (Rakita et al., 2018) for its two 6-DoF arms, and LocoMan-Dex2 reuses the whole-body controller and finite-state machine of Human2LocoMan (Niu et al., 2025), which convert the end-effector target of the active manipulator into joint commands.

Hand and gripper control.

For the Inspire hands of G1-Dex5 and the LEAP Hand of xArm7-Dex4, fingertip targets expressed in the wrist frame are converted into hand joint commands by DexPilot retargeting (Handa et al., 2020), using an implementation adapted from dex-retargeting (Qin et al., 2023). At every control step, the hand joint angles 𝒒\bm{q} are obtained by solving

min𝒒min≤𝒒≤𝒒max⁡1N​∑i=1Nwi​ℓsmooth-L1​(‖𝒗i​(𝒒)−𝒗^i‖2)+λs​‖𝒒−𝒒prev‖22+γ​‖𝒒‖22,\min_{\bm{q}_{\min}\leq\bm{q}\leq\bm{q}_{\max}}\;\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}\,\ell_{\text{smooth-L1}}\big(\|\bm{v}_{i}(\bm{q})-\hat{\bm{v}}_{i}\|_{2}\big)+\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\,\|\bm{q}-\bm{q}_{\mathrm{prev}}\|_{2}^{2}+\gamma\,\|\bm{q}\|_{2}^{2}, (20)

where 𝒗i​(𝒒)\bm{v}_{i}(\bm{q}) ranges over the NN wrist-to-fingertip and fingertip-to-fingertip vectors of the robot hand computed by forward kinematics, 𝒗^i\hat{\bm{v}}_{i} is the corresponding target vector, ℓsmooth-L1\ell_{\text{smooth-L1}} is the smooth L1 loss with a threshold of 3 cm, and 𝒒prev\bm{q}_{\mathrm{prev}} is the previous solution. Target vectors are the human vectors scaled by 1.2 for the Inspire hands and 1.6 for the LEAP Hand. As in DexPilot, a thumb–finger pair closer than 3 cm is treated as a pinch until the distance exceeds 5 cm. During a pinch, its target vector is shortened to 0.1 mm so that the fingertips make contact, and two fingers that pinch the thumb together while within 3 cm of each other are kept 3 cm apart. These projected vectors are weighted by wi=200w_{i}=200 and wi=400w_{i}=400, respectively, the remaining fingertip-to-fingertip vectors by wi=1w_{i}=1, and the wrist-to-fingertip vectors by wi=15w_{i}=15 for the Inspire hands and wi=10w_{i}=10 for the LEAP Hand. The second term, with λs=4×10−3\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}=4\times 10^{-3}, keeps consecutive solutions close. The last term is not part of dex-retargeting; following DexPilot, we add it to regularize the joint angles toward zero, which corresponds to an open hand. This reduces redundancy in the solution and keeps the hand out of poor local minima that are difficult to recover from, such as fingers embedded in the palm. We use γ=1.5×10−2\gamma=1.5\times 10^{-2}, whereas DexPilot uses γ=2.5×10−3\gamma=2.5\times 10^{-3} for the Allegro hand. The problem is solved with SLSQP, warm-started from the previous solution, and the resulting joint angles are smoothed by a first-order low-pass filter (α=0.2\alpha=0.2) before being sent to the hand.

For the grippers of R1Lite-Gripper and LocoMan-Dex2, the controller computes the distance between the two fingertip targets and maps it linearly to a gripper command, using the same map as teleoperation. On LocoMan-Dex2, distances from 2 to 15 cm map to gripper angles from 0.01 to 1.8 rad. On R1Lite-Gripper, distances from 0.8 to 15 cm map to the full gripper range; the command is low-pass filtered and then binarized, so the gripper opens fully when the distance exceeds about 5 cm and closes otherwise.

Body and base control.

On G1-Dex5, the predicted torso pose, consisting of torso height and orientation, and the velocity command, consisting of forward, lateral, and yaw velocities, are passed to the lower-body controller of Humanoid Touch Dream (Niu et al., 2026). This learned policy runs at 50 Hz and outputs targets for the 12 leg joints and 3 waist joints. On R1Lite-Gripper, the predicted velocity command drives the mobile chassis and is set to zero whenever the most recent command is older than 0.4 s.

A.8 Dataset and Data Collection

Dataset overview.

EgoX is trained on a heterogeneous collection of egocentric manipulation demonstrations spanning human, physical-robot, and simulated embodiments. In total, the dataset contains 4,851 trajectories corresponding to 34.38 hours of interaction. Table 6 summarizes the dataset composition for each embodiment, while Fig. 12 visualizes the task distribution across embodiments.

Data composition.

The dataset is deliberately heterogeneous in both embodiment and task composition. Human demonstrations constitute the largest source, with 2,396 trajectories (49.4% of the full dataset), while demonstrations collected on physical robots contribute 1,706 trajectories (35.2%). The remaining 749 trajectories (15.4%) are collected with the simulated G1 embodiment. Among the robot embodiments, G1-Dex5 and G1-Sim-Dex3 provide the largest individual datasets, with 710 and 749 trajectories, respectively, while the remaining platforms provide smaller but morphologically diverse sources of manipulation experience.

Importantly, the dataset is not constructed by replicating the same task set across every embodiment. Instead, different embodiments contribute different subsets of tasks according to their morphology and manipulation capabilities. Cross-embodiment overlap therefore arises through semantically corresponding observation and action modalities rather than requiring identical tasks or actuator-level action spaces across all platforms.

Data collection.

Similar to Human2LocoMan (Niu et al., 2025), both human and real-robot data are collected with an Apple Vision Pro that captures the operator’s head and hand motions, while simulated data are collected by teleoperation in simulation with PICO XR devices (Appendix A.11). The headset tracks the head pose and 25 keypoints per hand, and all streams are recorded at 30 Hz. Operators start and stop each episode with left-hand pinch gestures, thumb to index finger to start and thumb to middle finger to stop and reset, so no additional input device is needed. Each episode is stored as an HDF5 file with the available images, poses, proprioception, and actions.

Human demonstrations.

For human data, a stereo camera is rigidly mounted on the headset and records egocentric images as side-by-side stereo frames of 1280×4801280\times 480 pixels. The operator performs the task with their own hands while seeing the scene through the headset’s see-through mode (Park & Agrawal, 2024). The tracked wrist poses are expressed in the egocentric frame ℱego\mathcal{F}_{\text{ego}} (Sec. 3.1), and the five fingertips of each hand, expressed in the wrist frame, serve as the end-effector link keypoints.

Robot demonstrations.

Physical robots are teleoperated with the same headset. The operator’s wrist poses and hand keypoints are converted into targets in the unified egocentric frame system and streamed at 30 Hz to the robot, where the control stack of Appendix A.7 executes them. For grippers, the thumb–index pinch distance sets the gripper opening, and for G1-Dex5, the operator’s head orientation and changes in head height set the torso orientation and height. Base velocity commands are issued with a separate input device, the wireless remote of G1-Dex5 or a keyboard for the R1Lite-Gripper chassis, and are recorded from the robot state. The operator watches the robot’s stereo head-camera stream in the headset through an Open-TeleVision (Cheng et al., 2024) interface. Each recorded step stores the commanded targets as actions, together with the robot’s egocentric images and the poses and proprioception returned by the controller.

A.9 Task and Evaluation Protocol

We evaluate 13 task–embodiment pairs: Scoop on G1-Dex5, xArm7-Dex4, LocoMan-Dex2, and Z1-Tool; Sort on G1-Dex5, xArm7-Dex4, and R1Lite-Gripper; Insert on G1-Dex5 and xArm7-Dex4; Kitchen-Bread on G1-Dex5, R1Lite-Gripper, and G1-Sim-Dex3; and Kitchen-Cleanup on G1-Sim-Dex3. Figs. 13–17 show example rollouts of these pairs, grouped by task.

ID and OOD conditions.

Both conditions are defined for each task–embodiment pair with respect to its fine-tuning dataset, i.e., the demonstrations of the target task on the target embodiment, which are excluded from pretraining (Appendix A.3). In-distribution (ID) trials use settings drawn from the same distribution as the fine-tuning demonstrations, including the same objects and receptacles and the same range of initial object placements. Out-of-distribution (OOD) trials use configurations that are unseen in the fine-tuning dataset, such as new object shapes, sizes, and colors, a different receptacle, sauce, or plate, or new initial object placement, while the task goal and the stage scoring remain unchanged. The ID and OOD configurations of each pair are given after the description of each task below. Fig. 19 shows the real objects of each task, and Fig. 19 the object appearances in simulation.

OOD evaluation tests cross-embodiment transfer.

OOD configurations are absent from the target task–embodiment fine-tuning data. Some occur in the cross-embodiment pretraining mixture: in the demonstrations of other embodiments, most notably the human demonstrations, or in demonstrations of other tasks. A policy trained only on the target-embodiment data, such as ACT or MXT+ without pretraining, has therefore never observed these configurations, whereas a pretrained policy may have observed them while they were handled by a human or another robot. The OOD evaluation is designed to measure exactly this case: whether experience with a configuration on other embodiments, especially humans, transfers to a target robot that has never encountered it. This is the setting that cross-embodiment pretraining targets, and OOD results should be read as a test of cross-embodiment transfer rather than of generalization to configurations that are absent from all training data.

Scoop (cat litter scooping).

The scene contains a litter box filled with cat litter, a scoop resting on the edge of the box, and a disposal bin next to it. The robot grasps the scoop, moves it to the waste in the box, i.e., the target object, scoops and lifts it, empties it into the disposal bin, and returns the scoop to the edge of the box. On xArm7-Dex4 and Z1-Tool, the box stands on a table. On G1-Dex5, it is placed on the floor, so the humanoid lowers its torso to reach it, and LocoMan-Dex2 holds the scoop with the gripper on its front leg. Z1-Tool carries a scoop that is rigidly attached to the arm and therefore skips the grasp. ID and OOD. On all four embodiments, ID trials use a white disposal bin within the position range seen in fine-tuning, and OOD trials replace it with a green disposal bin or move it to new positions. On G1-Dex5, xArm7-Dex4, and Z1-Tool, whose workspaces are large, OOD trials also place the waste at new positions in the litter box.

Sort (block sorting).

Red and blue building blocks lie on the table in front of a red and a blue bin, whose left–right order varies across trials. The robot picks up each block and places it into the bin of the same color. Each block is scored independently, and approaching or placing into the wrong bin earns only partial credit (Table 7). The bimanual G1-Dex5 and R1Lite-Gripper use both arms. ID and OOD. ID trials use three blocks of the shapes seen in the fine-tuning data, and each reproduces the initial layout of a recorded demonstration. On all three embodiments, OOD trials use blocks of new shapes, e.g., a four-stud brick. On R1Lite-Gripper, OOD trials also change the number of blocks, e.g., to four.

Insert (T-shaped block insertion).

A T-shaped block lies on the table next to a fixed base with a T-shaped slot. The robot approaches and grasps the block, reorients and aligns it with the slot, and inserts it; a near-successful insertion earns partial credit. ID and OOD. ID trials use the block seen in the fine-tuning data, which is light purple on G1-Dex5 and white on xArm7-Dex4. On xArm7-Dex4, the block is placed at nine predefined positions, one of which is repeated four more times. OOD trials on G1-Dex5 use a white block, a dark purple block, or a larger brown block, and OOD trials on xArm7-Dex4 use the light purple block or the larger brown block. For each embodiment, the OOD evaluation uses blocks demonstrated by the other embodiment during cross-embodiment pretraining.

Kitchen-Bread (sauce spreading).

This long-horizon task combines locomotion with manipulation. On G1-Dex5, the robot opens the refrigerator, grasps the sauce container, closes the refrigerator, walks to the counter, and places the container next to a plate of bread. It then picks up the spreading tool, dips it into the sauce, spreads the sauce onto the bread, and puts the tool back. On R1Lite-Gripper, the robot picks up the sauce container from a counter instead of a refrigerator, drives its wheeled base to the table with the bread, places the container, and performs the same spreading steps. G1-Sim-Dex3 performs the G1-Dex5 sequence in the simulated kitchen (Appendix A.11). ID and OOD. On G1-Dex5, ID trials use white condensed milk and brown bread on a green plate, and OOD trials use another kind of condensed milk and a blue plate, with white or brown bread. On R1Lite-Gripper, ID trials use white condensed milk and brown bread, and OOD trials use a different sauce, e.g., mayonnaise or strawberry jam, or white condensed milk on white bread; the plate is the same in both conditions. On G1-Sim-Dex3, ID trials sample object appearances and layouts from the demonstration distribution. OOD trials use unseen object and scene appearances, together with unseen plate–spreader layouts (Appendix A.11).

Kitchen-Cleanup (tool organization).

This task is evaluated only on G1-Sim-Dex3. A spreader rests on a plate on the counter next to a container, and the robot grasps the spreader and places it into the container. ID and OOD. ID trials sample appearances and layouts from the demonstration distribution. OOD trials use object and scene appearances not present in those demonstrations (Appendix A.11).

Trials and scoring.

Each real-world pair is evaluated over 20 trials (13 ID and 7 OOD), and each simulated pair over 50 trials (32 ID and 18 OOD). All methods are evaluated on the same trial configurations. We score each trial with a stage-based task progress score that gives partial credit for intermediate stages. For a trial with accumulated stage score ss, success indicator b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}, and task-specific maximum score SmaxS_{\max} including the success bonus, the normalized task progress score is P=(s+b)/SmaxP=(s+b)/S_{\max}. Table 7 lists the stages, points, and success criteria of each task. ID and OOD scores are reported separately.

A.10 Success Rates

Sec. 4 reports the normalized task progress score PP. Fig. 20 reports the success rate on the same trials, i.e., the fraction of trials with b=1b=1 (Appendix A.9), for each method and task–embodiment pair under ID and OOD conditions.

Success rates give the same overall ranking as task progress. Averaged over the 13 pairs, cross-embodiment pretraining raises the success rate of MXT+ from 0.35 to 0.56 and improves 11 of 13 pairs, while π0.5\pi_{0.5} and ACT reach 0.27 and 0.11. The gain is largest out of distribution: there, MXT+ without pretraining succeeds no more often than π0.5\pi_{0.5} (0.18 vs. 0.19), and pretraining raises it to 0.52, compared with a rise from 0.44 to 0.58 in distribution. Embodiment dreaming likewise raises the success rate over MXT in all seven settings of Fig. 7, from 0.39 to 0.62 on average (from 0.46 to 0.63 in distribution and from 0.27 to 0.60 out of distribution), most on G1-Dex5 Scoop (from 3 to 16 of 20 trials).

A.11 Simulation Details

Simulation setup.

We simulate G1-Sim-Dex3, a Unitree G1 humanoid with three-finger Dex3 hands, in a kitchen environment built in Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab. In Kitchen-Bread, the robot retrieves a sauce can from the refrigerator, carries it to the worktop, and spreads its contents onto bread; the shorter Kitchen-Cleanup task requires picking up the spreader and placing it in a container. Objects interact through rigid-body contact, while sauce transfer is rendered visually without fluid simulation. Demonstrations are collected by teleoperation with PICO controllers, and the egocentric head-camera and wrist-camera images are rendered offline with RTX. Physics runs at 200​Hz200\,\mathrm{Hz} and the locomotion controller at 50​Hz50\,\mathrm{Hz}.

Randomization.

At reset, we randomize the robot and object positions, object sizes, aisle width, and worktop height, keep the spreader supported by the plate, and check each sampled layout for clearance. We also vary the bread shape and the positions of background objects and furniture. During offline rendering, we randomize object and room materials, lighting, camera poses and fields of view, and image properties such as color, noise, blur, and compression. These visual changes leave the recorded motions and action labels unchanged. Each rendered episode uses a fixed visual configuration, with noise varying across frames, and the dataset also retains variants close to the original appearance. Fig. 19 shows the object appearances, including those used only in OOD trials.

Evaluation.

Each task is evaluated on 50 fixed trials: 32 ID and 18 OOD. OOD trials use object and scene appearances excluded from the demonstrations; Kitchen-Bread OOD trials also include plate–spreader arrangements outside the demonstrated range. Trial configurations were refined through pilot evaluations and then fixed for all methods. Kitchen-Bread and Kitchen-Cleanup trials last 90 and 45 simulated seconds, respectively. Actions are executed at 30​Hz30\,\mathrm{Hz}. MXT+ and ACT execute 45 actions before each new prediction, while π0.5\pi_{0.5} uses RTC (Appendix A.4). Kitchen-Bread success requires spreading sauce onto the bread and, at the end of the trial, a released spreader settled on a support. Kitchen-Cleanup success requires grasping the spreader and placing it inside the container, released and supported, at any point during the trial. We score nine prerequisite-dependent stages for Kitchen-Bread and four for Kitchen-Cleanup, plus one point for success, giving maximum scores of 10 and 5; normalizing by these maxima gives the task progress score reported in Sec. 4.
